title: Half tablets: only when the stem says the tablet is scored
blurb: Give half tablets when, and only when, the tablet is scored, and type answers such as 1.5 and 0.5 correctly.
question: A person is prescribed bisoprolol 3.75 mg. The tablets in stock contain bisoprolol 2.5 mg and are scored. How many tablets should be given?

teach.body: Formal rule: a calculated part tablet may be given only when the tablet is scored (made with a break line so it splits into equal halves). Plain English: if the question says the tablet is scored, 1.5 or 0.5 tablets is a valid answer; if it does not, a half answer means you need a different strength or have made an error. Part A practice papers used whole numbers, so half tablets are stretch items and the stem will say "scored".
teach.cite: Pearson VUE NMC practice papers; FACTS.md section 5 (rounding)

teach.caption: Quarters and thirds are not given by splitting: they signal an error or a need for a liquid.

teach.h: Worked example: Mr Nowak on a rehabilitation ward
teach.body: Tomasz Nowak, 72, is prescribed bisoprolol 3.75 mg. The stock is bisoprolol 2.5 mg tablets, which the box says are scored. Want ÷ have = 3.75 ÷ 2.5 = 1.5 tablets: one whole tablet and one half. Sense-check: 2.5 mg + 1.25 mg = 3.75 mg. You type 1.5.

teach.text: Rounding a half tablet to a whole number (1.5 to 2, or 0.5 to 1) gives a wrong dose. A scored-tablet answer is typed exactly: 1.5, not 2 and not 1.

teach.h: If the tablet is not scored
teach.body: When a calculation gives 1.5 but the tablets are not scored, do not split them. Look for a combination of strengths that makes the dose in whole tablets (for example a 5 mg plus a 2.5 mg tablet), or ask the pharmacist about a liquid. In the exam the stem tells you what is in stock.

items: Half tablets only when the stem says the tablet is scored.
Do not round the result: 1.5 stays 1.5.
Type halves with a leading zero and no trailing zero: 0.5, 1.5.
A quarter or a third of a tablet signals an error or a different formulation.
Unscored: make the dose from whole tablets of the strengths stocked.

summary: You can now decide when a half tablet is allowed, calculate scored-tablet doses without rounding, and type answers like 0.5 and 1.5 in Pearson's format. You can also build a dose from whole tablets when the tablets are not scored.

A.q: A person is prescribed 15 mg of a medicine. The tablets available contain 10 mg each and are scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
A.why: Want ÷ have = 15 mg ÷ 10 mg = 1.5 tablets. The tablets are scored, so one and a half tablets is allowed.

whyNot.0: Rounded up: 2 tablets would give 20 mg.
whyNot.3: Rounded down: 1 tablet would give 10 mg.

A.q: You have a prescription for 50 mg of a medicine. The tablets available contain 100 mg each and are scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
A.why: Want ÷ have = 50 mg ÷ 100 mg = 0.5 tablets: half a scored tablet. Typed with a leading zero: 0.5.

whyNot.0: Inverted fraction: have ÷ want gives 2 tablets (200 mg).
whyNot.1: Rounded up to a whole tablet, giving 100 mg.
whyNot.2: 100 mg was misread as 10 mg, giving 5 tablets.

A.q: A person is prescribed 12.5 mg of a medicine. The tablets available contain 5 mg each and are scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
A.why: Want ÷ have = 12.5 mg ÷ 5 mg = 2.5 tablets. Scored, so two and a half tablets.

whyNot.1: Rounded up: 3 tablets would give 15 mg.
whyNot.2: Rounded down: 2 tablets would give 10 mg.

B.q: A person is prescribed 0.75 mg of a medicine. Each tablet contains 0.5 mg and is scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: 0.5 mg was misread as 0.05 mg, giving 15.

B.q: A person is prescribed 125 micrograms of a medicine. The tablets available contain 0.25 mg each and are scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
B.why: Convert: 0.25 mg = 250 micrograms. Want ÷ have = 125 ÷ 250 = 0.5 tablets.

whyNot.2: 0.25 mg was taken as 25 micrograms, giving 5.
whyNot.3: 0.25 mg was taken as 2500 micrograms, giving 0.05.

B.q: A patient is prescribed 300 mg of a medicine. The tablets available contain 200 mg each and are scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.2: Divided by 100 mg, not the 200 mg on the label.

C.q: A person is prescribed 45 mg of a medicine a day in two equal doses. The tablets available contain 15 mg each and are scored. How many tablets should be given for each dose? Write your answer to one decimal place.
C.why: One dose = 45 mg ÷ 2 = 22.5 mg. Tablets = 22.5 ÷ 15 = 1.5 tablets per dose.

whyNot.0: This is the number of tablets for the whole day (3), not each dose.
whyNot.2: Rounded 1.5 up to 2 tablets (30 mg per dose).

C.q: A person is prescribed 7.5 mg of a medicine. The stock holds 5 mg tablets and 2.5 mg tablets, and neither is scored. What is the fewest number of whole tablets that gives the dose?
C.why: One 5 mg tablet plus one 2.5 mg tablet = 7.5 mg in 2 tablets. Neither tablet may be split.

whyNot.0: 1.5 of a 5 mg tablet needs splitting, but the tablets are not scored.
whyNot.1: Three 2.5 mg tablets is the right dose, but not the fewest tablets.

C.q: A person is prescribed 0.0625 mg of a medicine. The tablets available contain 125 micrograms each and are scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
C.why: Convert: 0.0625 mg × 1000 = 62.5 micrograms. Want ÷ have = 62.5 ÷ 125 = 0.5 tablets.

whyNot.2: 0.0625 mg was taken as 625 micrograms, a tenfold slip giving 5.
whyNot.3: 0.0625 mg was taken as 6.25 micrograms, giving 0.05.

reteach.title: Scored means halves are allowed
reteach.question: The sum gives 1.5 tablets and the stem says the tablets are scored. What do you give?

blocks.body: Scored tablets break cleanly in half, so 1.5 tablets is one whole tablet and one half. Do not round to 2 or 1: each changes the dose by a third or more.

blocks.text: "Rounding to a whole tablet to be safe" is not safe: it changes the dose. Split only scored tablets, and only into halves.

explain.body: The stem tells you whether the tablet is scored. If it is, a half answer is valid: type it exactly.

test.q: A person is prescribed 20 mg of a medicine. The tablets available contain 40 mg each and are scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
test.why: Want ÷ have = 20 mg ÷ 40 mg = 0.5 tablets: half a scored tablet.

whyNot.1: Rounded up to one tablet (40 mg).
whyNot.2: Divided by 80 mg, double the label strength, giving 0.25.

test.q: A person is prescribed 37.5 mg of a medicine. Each tablet contains 25 mg and is scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.

items.label: marked wrong on the practice test

test.q: A person is prescribed 2 mg of a medicine. The tablets available contain 4 mg each and are scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
test.why: Want ÷ have = 2 mg ÷ 4 mg = 0.5 tablets, typed as 0.5.

whyNot.1: Rounded up to one tablet (4 mg).
whyNot.3: 4 mg was misread as 40 mg, giving 0.05.

explain.body: If the units differ, convert first. 0.375 g = 375 mg; then want ÷ have as usual.

test.q: A patient is prescribed 0.375 g of a medicine. The tablets available contain 250 mg each and are scored. How many tablets should be given? Write your answer to one decimal place.
test.why: Convert: 0.375 g × 1000 = 375 mg. Want ÷ have = 375 ÷ 250 = 1.5 tablets.

whyNot.1: 0.375 g was taken as 3750 mg, a tenfold slip giving 15.
whyNot.2: 0.375 g was taken as 37.5 mg, giving 0.15.
